meta.title: Lydian: Major With the Fourth Raised
meta.summary: Lydian is A major with one degree raised, its characteristic note is the #4, and its vamp is two major triads a whole tone apart that share no notes at all.

spans.text: The avoid-note lesson left this exactly here: Lydian's raised fourth is the one degree in this chapter that removes Ionian's clash altogether. So what is Lydian actually like, once that one liability is gone? Start with what changed.

Lydian keeps the leading tone. It and Ionian are the only two of the seven modes with a
sitting a half step below home —

counted that membership already. Raising the fourth cost Lydian nothing on that front: the leading tone is untouched, the same note in the same place Ionian keeps it. So Lydian isn't major loosened up — it's major with the leading tone still there, minus the one note that used to grate.
Its tritone is measured off the root itself,

already gave this address: Lydian is the only one of this chapter's three whose tritone touches the tonic at all. (Locrian's does too, elsewhere in the family — that's not a claim about all seven.) Ionian's tritone missed the tonic triad completely; Lydian's sits right on the root, which is a very different kind of tension to carry into a chord that isn't moving.

The app's own line for this card is "Major with a ♯4 — weightless, floating", and that's the register worth borrowing: film scoring and a strand of rock are where you've actually heard this, not a property the interval carries on its own.
